successor: Kingdom of Germany under the Ottonians (same East Frankish kingship)
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Henry I, king of Germany' - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Henry-I-king-of-Germany
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Conrad I, king of Germany' - https://www.britannica.com/biography/Conrad-I-king-of-Germany
notes: Conrad I (911-18) fought the dukes of Saxony, Bavaria and Swabia and lost Lotharingia. He designated Henry of Saxony, elected king in 919. The same East Frankish kingship continued, so the database break is a relabelling.

successor: Hawaii III (Hawaii Island chiefdom under Umi-a-Liloa)
source1: Kirch, P.V., How Chiefs Became Kings: Divine Kingship and the Rise of Archaic States in Ancient Hawaii, University of California Press - https://www.ucpress.edu/books/how-chiefs-became-kings/paper
source2: Hommon, R.J., The Ancient Hawaiian State: Origins of a Political Society, Oxford University Press, 2013 - https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ancient-hawaiian-state-9780199916122
notes: The c.1580 break fits Umi-a-Liloa's usurpation of his half-brother Hakau and unification of the island within the same ruling line. Sources describe chiefdoms turning into states internally. Umi's dates are disputed (c.1490-1600).

source1: Mukhtar, M.H., Historical Dictionary of Somalia, Scarecrow Press, 2003 (chronology/introduction) - https://archive.org/details/historical-dictionary-of-somaalia-maxamed-xaaji-mukhtaar/mode/2up
source2: No second accessible scholarly source found on how the Tunni polity ended
notes: The 'Tunni Sultanate' is poorly attested. Accessible scholarly sources confirm only that the Tunni lived in the lower Shabelle valley. Claims that Garen/Ajuran conquered it in the 13th century rest on uncited popular accounts. Dates unverifiable.

source1: Chowdhury, A.M., Dynastic History of Bengal (c.750-1200 A.D.), Asiatic Society of Pakistan, Dacca, 1967 (preface and ch. I note) - https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.148627
source2: No second accessible scholarly source (Banglapedia entries unreachable)
notes: Chandra rule at Vikramapura lasted to the mid-11th century, then the Varmans rose. Chola (c.1021-24) and Kalachuri Karna invasions came first. The Varmans, outsiders tied to Karna, took control. Mode inferred; some accounts claim Pala annexation.

successor: Sultanate of Geledi (Gobroon dynasty) and Hiraab Imamate
source1: Mukhtar, M.H., Historical Dictionary of Somalia, Scarecrow Press, 2003 (introduction: Ajuran authority over riverine region in 16th-17th c., seat at Marka) - https://archive.org/details/historical-dictionary-of-somaalia-maxamed-xaaji-mukhtaar/mode/2up
source2: No second accessible scholarly source (Cassanelli 1982 and Luling 2002 not accessible)
notes: Late-17th-century revolts against Ajuran taxation split the realm: Geledi overthrew Ajuran clients at Afgooye, and the Abgaal Hiraab Imamate took Mogadishu. Coded internal. Marka's fate is unclear, and the end is late 17th century, not exactly 1700.

successor: Ethiopia Kingdom II (Solomonic monarchy, Gondarine period)
notes: The Solomonic monarchy continued: Susenyos (1607-32) abdicated in favour of his son Fasilides, who founded Gondar. 1620 is a period break, not an end. Succession wars and opposition to Catholic conversion came before the break.

The Bito were Bunyoro's royal dynasty. A British expedition took Kabarega's headquarters, deposing him in 1894; Bunyoro joined the protectorate in 1896. Q4: the 1869-70 succession war. Bito kings later ruled as British clients.

successor: Wari Empire (colony at Pikillacta); local Cuzco communities continued
source1: Belisle, V., 'Understanding Wari State Expansion: A Bottom-Up Approach at the Village of Ak'awillay, Cusco, Peru', Latin American Antiquity 26(2), 2015 - https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/latin-american-antiquity/article/abs/understanding-wari-state-expansion-a-bottomup-approach-at-the-village-of-akawillay-cusco-peru/8B78785C59154EA392FD2C415114259B
notes: Cuzco's Early Intermediate is a material-culture phase with no recorded central authority. From c.600-650 Wari colonists (Pikillacta) had minimal impact on local villages, and Wari held only the area near the colony. Local settlement continued.

source1: Xin Tangshu (New Tang History), juan 219, Shiwei section (primary source) - https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%96%B0%E5%94%90%E6%9B%B8/%E5%8D%B7219
source2: No second accessible scholarly source found
notes: Xin Tangshu: no overall ruler, only 20+ tribes under chiefs, northeast of the Turks, not in the Orkhon. Some tribes were absorbed by the Khitan around 900; others moved west. No single ending; database location and dates look wrong.

successor: Monte Alban III (same Zapotec state at Monte Alban)
source2: Spencer, C.S. and Redmond, E.M., 'Primary State Formation in Mesoamerica', Annual Review of Anthropology 33, 2004 - https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.anthro.33.070203.143823
notes: II/IIIA is a ceramic-phase boundary. Monte Alban stayed the Zapotec centre, flourished in Period III and lost its pre-eminence only in Period IV (after c.800). The Oaxaca state existed by Period II. No break at AD 200.
